title: Inkling 2 Mini (thinkingmachines.ai)
comments: This is bonkers good if these benchmarks hold up in real-world scenarios.  To be at the level of Qwen3.8-27B with a looped transformer model is quite the flex.  They just left this note on reddit:Hope that folks find this model more amenable to local usage - the sizing was largely informed by what folks on this subreddit ask for the most haha!There are two particularly interesting aspects of this model for local users:We do our training end-to-end in nvfp4, and although we haven't exhaustively benchmarked this, folks like Unsloth have noticed that our models seem to respond very well to being quantized, maintaining 90% top-1 even at at 1-bit quantization.This model is looped, which allows more depth at the same parameter count, which we particularly notice seems helpful for coding tasks. :)This is our first model targeted at local users, so let us know how this model is and anything you want to see out of future iterations!https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1y1diuk/thinkin...reply

> This is bonkers good if these benchmarks hold up in real-world scenariosI think we’re going to start seeing a lot more of these types of advances, especially on smaller modelsI’ve been able to graft reasoning and math problem solving into a small, locally trained model with 6.5M params. And I’ve also been able to add abilities or improve them by “growing” the model to 8.5M params (this usually means redistributing the weights in a slightly different network size, then finetune the new size)The model is so small that I can sometimes run dozens of experiments per day. There are a lot of papers and new models coming out. A lot of the stuff they are doing at 100B-1T still works at smaller scale (usually not the scaling inference-related optimizations, but rather things like weight programming, or a “looped” architecture). It’s a lot of fun to run at home on my laptopI imagine bigger labs with bigger budgets (more GPUs) are mostly focused on 20B-1T+ models. But there’s a lot to explore in local “home models”reply

People have been saying this since we first started having local models … that were too big to run locally.It would be great if it was true.Running a local frontier model is the dream.…but, its been obvious since the beginning that this is a fantasy without a paradigm shift.People want general purpose models. People want parallel models. People want fast models.This is interesting, because it does represent a paradigm shift, perhaps… but most people saying “Ive been expecting this…” have simply not had a realistic understanding of complexities involved.Personally; Im skeptical. This is what people were saying about 1 bit models. That turned out to make very little meaningful diff and did not result in a local hosting utopia.I guess we will see… I feel like we will see slow incremental improvements in this space.Sub 1B coding models remains a fantasy for now.reply

When people started saying this, top-end frontier models were dumber than this model is. It's just that the frontier moves forward so fast that by the time the "paradigm shift" happens of small models being usable, there's a new batch of frontier models that open an entirely different paradigm that small models cannot contest.reply

I think that will remain the case for general purpose coding, however we might be able to train very focused coding models in that size. For example, a model that's only focused on coding Python - maybe that could fit in 1B params?reply
> Sub 1B coding models remains a fantasy for now.For sure, and it will continue to be so, until it isn’tIn the meantime, I think there’s a lot of encouraging developmentsreply
This is the first I’m hearing of a looped model. What is it?reply

It's a pretty broad bucket that contains a few different research lineages, but the gist (when talking about Transformers) is that instead of stacking 12 latent blocks, you can stack 4 and let them loop 3 times.That's just a general simplification though. One of the key motivators in this general area of research is adaptive latent reasoning, meaning in theory, some tasks only require 2 loops and some require 8.There's a lot of different approaches here and many of them approach the problem from different traditions. Some looped transformers use a fixed loop count, others follow after deep equilibrium models and iterate towards a fixed point or some other stopping mechanism.Some fun reading if you're interested in this field:- TinyRecursiveModels - Blew up a couple of years ago when it performed really well on ARC AGI 1 using a comparatively small model with a large task-level table of embedding prefixes. https://github.com/samsungsailmontreal/tinyrecursivemodels- Sebastian Raschka's piece on the general architecture patterns we see today: https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/looped...reply

A couple other benefits aside from adaptive reasoning:- It lets the model do more of its reasoning without emitting tokens. This is helpful both because a) insanely long token streams are annoying, but more importantly b) long reasoning streams eat context. It's not a direct performance enhancement, since each token is more expensive to generate (you need to loop!), but it reduces spam in the context window which likely translates into some degree of intelligence win for multi-turn since the model won't have to sift through as much noise, and it'll need to compact less frequently per task which is also likely an indirect intelligence win and an indirect cost/perf win per task: post-compaction re-reads of files are basically useless spam to an inference engine, so if you could do the entire task within one context window, you'd hit the engine less per task.- It lets potentially every token use more computation, instead of keeping the test-time-compute scaling purely in the upfront CoT domain. While it's helpful to think upfront, it can be useful to think mid-stream too.Overall it's potentially much better.reply

Yes, and for others' reference, Astra is the one SOTA model known to be looped.Looping is controversial among the alignment/safey crowd, because the more models can think without printing a trace, the less understandable they might be to us.reply

title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them (manidoraisamy.com)
comments: Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.reply

> Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed?Yes, that is how most functional organizations operate.Architects are a bad meme, along the same lines as scrum masters and product managers.
Good software engineers spend more time on design than implementation, and the best are helping their teammates with design, and auditing designs of adjacent teams to ensure integration success.
So architecture is an important part of the job, but that doesn't mean that you can automatically declare a role with the title "architect" and make the whole organization better at design.Architect roles are a bad meme because the architect always ends up knowing less about the system and how it is used than the engineers and support staff, yet they have more influence over the decisions affecting those things.  That's the essence of an organizational anti-pattern/bad-meme any time it shows up: influence over resources anti-correlated with decision quality.
Additionally, architects often report to non-technical folks fairly high up the chain.  Those people are bad at screening for such a technical role, sometimes even making the mistake of replacing an architect with an external hire.reply

Good architects delegate down and are there to ensure the big picture remains consistent while leaving the teams to sweat the details because they are closer to the problem.Bad architects try to micromanage and those are the cases where you end up with systems that are slow and unworkable with processes that have too much ceremony.reply

When in that role I focus on supporting the team.  Mentoring, resolving disagreements, providing broader context, suggesting more options to consider (often stuff we could copy from older systems), etc.The main area where I spend influence on really shape the outcome is on process and team culture, not any specific technical decision.reply

Organizations that where dysfunctional in the past will keep growing these structures only that now the complexity will increase much much faster because teams can do (vibecode) so much more.reply

I've always treated the architect role as more setting broad goals, defining boundaries for individual ownership, and technical dispute resolution.  Sort of what you see with a lot of directors of movies where you get the best work by empowering individuals to completely own a carefully built little box that is a brick in the larger work.Those could be done by normal management, but I've found it better to separate those discussions from management style discussions.  Sort of like how the BDFL role in a large open source project is rarely anyone's actual boss.Albeit, I'm still recalibrating what all this means in an agentic world.  It makes sense with the little swarm I directly command, but the pressures for downstream ICs to ignore the art and taste of what they're doing is more than a bit unfortunate since the core of what I'm saying is to empower them to give a shit and be proud about what they built.reply

All software development is architecture. Decide to implement a change by adding an if block to some code, by adding a function, by creating a new module and implementing it there, locally in the browser or on the server… those are all architectural decisions.Large scale software development is just a nested series of architectural choices from top to bottom.That some organizations choose to give some software developers the job title of architect is not a ‘bad meme’, it’s a reaction to the realization that there’s a lot of architectural decisions being made and it might be nice if all the people making them had sufficient information to make them right.Good ‘architects’ focus on making sure developers who are making all those architectural decisions have the right context to make them.Bad ‘architects’ try to make - or preempt, or second guess - all those decisions that have to be made. That doesn’t scale and doesn’t work.reply

title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (terrytao.wordpress.com)
comments: Something I don’t quite know, maybe someone closer to math can answer this questionIt seems we’re making tremendous progress on the back of existing abstractions and concepts with the brute force ability to generate language and verify proofs.For example, Tao says about the Riemann proof:> appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometryWhat I wonder: how do we create new abstractions and concepts? Like whatever “Langlands program” is? That then feedback into the system, and allow for even more sophisticated mathematics.Are we assuming AI will do this? Or does this still need to be something at least agreed-upon by a mathematics community - in the same way programmers talk about a “linked list” without having an hour long conversation to define it axiomatically? And without that social aspect, without breaking down long proofs into Lego block common abstractions, math may plateau? In part because we lose the ability to ask meaningful questions?reply

The recent progress in AI maths I think has made it a lot more obvious and visible what maths is at its core: The study of interesting patterns that emerge from the consistent application of simple rules.It's quite similar to the Game of Life and the community around it that tries to find interesting ever fancier gliders in that way.The thing about maths though is that what counts as big and interesting is socially determined and chosen by the community over decades or centuries.It remains to be seen whether human mathematicians will be content with also having the AI decide what's interesting.One possibility I suppose is to find an objective definition of what's interesting, e.g. some sort of centrality score to a theorem within the tree of theorems it enables.reply

Their rough summaries on what is needed to solve them usually go:> Hodge: not a clue> BSD: not a clue> RH: not a clue> P vs NP: not a clue> Yang-Mills: "Well..."https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50252673So if we're in "not a clue" territory, maybe that's that.I fear that it gets muddled again with e.g. the concurrent human announcement and that in retrospect RH turns out to be easier than expected, like many other problems before.Math is hard, but how hard math is is also hard...reply

CAVEMAN SUMMARY: AI no need theory, only people need. Fable understand OpenAI math. Fable explain well to human. People the problem, not AI.I was reading a mathematician's take on a recent OpenAI proof (their area of expertise). They argued that models don't lack theory building, they just work at such a high level of abstraction that they don't need it.Theory is for us, so we can understand what the models are doing. They gave the example of Fable, which understood and explained everything perfectly right away (written by OpenAI's unreleased model in terse mathematical notiations).This was totally intuitive for the AI (Fable), but it took this person two weeks just to get a high-level grasp of it. Likely things humans have not conceived, but I believe will truly advance understanding. Post-train the existing models with that knowledge, and see them resolve these same problems with far less effort.Just a hunch. I'm neither an AI researcher nor a mathematician.reply

Open question - are these proofs brute forcing, or are they generating new theory at a level of abstraction and complexity we can't understand?Controversial statement: I think we've always done math by generalising from concrete experience. So concepts like numbers, spaces, shapes, distances, and curvature are based on physical experiences we use as anchors before expanding them far beyond physicality and looking for patterns in the abstractions.If AI is generalising from patterns in latent space, that's a different kind of abstraction, and one that's much more alien to us, because it's going to be much, much bigger - too big to fit inside even the smartest human mind.So AI theories and abstractions may be valid in true/false terms, but we will never be able to comprehend them in their raw form - just as we can't experience latent space directly, and will only experience tiny slices of it as outputs to our queries.reply

title: Valkey kills the skiplist, cuts sorted set overhead by up to 43% (valkey.io)
comments: I have to say I was always on the fence about Bill Pugh (Mr Skiplist).Some of his concurrency ideas were pretty good but Skip Lists were about the same time I was realizing that theoretical and practical design for performance had diverged and skip lists were a huge cache miss liability.It didn't hurt that a few people I was aware had tried them had gone back to something else due to live performance analysis being negative or inconclusive (If you can't prove one thing is better than the other, you use the simpler one, and skiplists are not simple)reply

B+tree were designed around optimized IO in the era of magnetic storage, they're inherently cache-friendly. Skiplists are the same thing as a b+tree but the structure is inverted, which makes skiplists more to concurrent writer-friendly than b+trees. Different tradeoffs.reply

But more cache misses, due to the variable pointer length structure.That cost varies from chip generation to generation, but it does seem to be the case that b trees win in more generations than they lose.reply

If AI disrupts an industry that previously had high wages and now can be automated by commodity AI products, would it not actually lower GDP in some way (initially anyway)? What I mean is, if you had an industry that was worth say $1 billion, but now that same industry could be automated and done cheaply then it is no longe worth $1 billion? In some ways this is beneficial to the economy in that has reduced the cost of this industry and so customers see a benefit of cheaper products, but how would it benefit say AI companies since they are not capturing a $1 billion industry, but instead sort of destroying a $1 billion industry? If they just keep commoditizing industries and there is ample competition between AI companies, then how is the AI company capturing value such that they would be worth as much money as people are saying they are worth (trillions of dollars)? Over the long term the economy will grow. That I am 100% confident of. When you take previously scarce resources and commoditize them, the knock on effects tend to spread widely. Intelligence and automation used to be enormously expensive, and now they are becoming cheaper by the day. Right now, frontier LLMs, which I consider wildly inefficient can give you mostly functional blueprints and diagrams for working products, like basic electronics on top of the image generation and code generation that is increasingly being commoditized.The goods and services built atop "tech" should start to become cheaper as well. For knowledge workers this is terrible, but for consumers, this is great. I think folks worrying about an economic collapse are only looking at this from the perspective of knowledge workers and not from the much larger population of consumers.The effect on the AI companies with pure competition is to make them basically worthless unless they find ways of stifling competition. For example by banning open weight AI in the name of safety, forming a global monopoly, buying up all the RAM capacity in the world, etc. All of this stuff is going on right now.The value is there. The true question is whether the wealth will be concentrated and captured or released and distributed. I'm in the camp the likely outcome is actually the former. A huge amount of the wealth of AI has not really been unlocked yet... consumer robotics, disease cures, universal constructor type machines. Furthermore, once we reach superintelligence, eventually someone will inevitably fuck up by letting the dam break by ablitering a model in the wrong way. This will give governments and companies rationale to lock up the best AI to develop frontier level IP.reply

The related economic concept here is the Broken Window Fallacy. Doing 'redundant' work doesn't improve the economy, because there's an opportunity cost doing to anything. And replacing the need to "fix broken windows" or do now-AI-automated work would free up that opportunity cost. Which is how it's worked for nearly all automation. (Though Computers are subject to long running debate about this. See the Solow Productivity Paradox)The gigawatt-sized asterisk on all of this is that AI companies have to capture that $1 billion. Anthropic has to ten-fold increase it's revenues or it goes bankrupt under it's current commitments. It has to increase it's revenues another 10 times to reach the $10,000,000,000,000/yr revenue required to support it's current valuation.Anthropic put their Total Addressable Market at 35% of Global GDP (~$40 trillion/yr). They're planning to capture all of the money.The second gigawatt-sized asterisk is that because of the fine handiwork of Mr. Huang, China has made very competitive AI models available for free, so the actual ability for AI companies to capture the value of the labour they displace ends up being quite limited. Thus a problem in the predictions: Something as to break, but it is as of yet unclear what that will be. Maybe Chinese AI will be banned, maybe Anthropic & OpenAI go bankrupt.reply
